narration: Start with a simple question: could life exist in an ocean that has never seen the sky?
On Jupiter's moon Europa, a global saltwater ocean lies hidden beneath a completely frozen crust.
That crust is tens of miles thick, and the ocean surface beneath it is frozen solid.
Yet the ocean underneath holds more than twice as much water as all of Earth's oceans combined.
It stays liquid not because of sunlight, but because Jupiter's gravity flexes the moon and heats it from within.
Sunlight never reaches that water, so nothing down there has ever seen a sunrise.
So the question becomes sharper: what could live in a dark ocean sealed under ice?
Europa is not even the only one: Saturn's moon Enceladus hides a global salty ocean beneath its icy crust.
Enceladus even sprays that ocean into space through cracks near its south pole.
On Earth, we already know what life can do without sunlight, because the deep sea has an answer.
This episode follows that answer outward, from a vent on our own sea floor to an ocean we have never touched.
Some of what follows is measured, and some of it is invented, and we will mark the difference every time.
By the end, you can decide which parts you believe.
Two of the least remarkable-looking moons in the solar system may be the most interesting.
Begin with the shape of the world: an ocean with no shore you could walk out onto, capped by ice.
Europa's ocean is global, which means it wraps the entire moon.
There is no beach here, no coastline, no place where water meets air.
Above the water sits a crust of ice tens of miles thick.
That ice stays frozen where it meets the water, so the boundary is a lid, not a shoreline.
The water below is the striking part: more than twice the volume of every ocean on Earth.
Twice over, in a single moon.
Volume is not the same as habitability, but it does buy room.
Room for chemistry, room for gradients, room for time.
The heat that keeps it liquid comes from Jupiter, which pulls on Europa as the moon orbits.
That flexing bends the moon, and the bending becomes heat.
Tidal heating is why the ocean is not a block of ice all the way through.
It also drives chemistry between the ocean and the rocky floor beneath it.
Enceladus, at Saturn, is smaller but follows the same logic.
It too carries a global salty ocean under an icy crust.
Two moons, two oceans, both sealed away from the sky.
If you wanted to design a place where life could hide, you would struggle to do better.
But hiding is not the same as living, and for that a world needs an energy source.
So the next thing to measure is not the size of the ocean, but what powers it.
Keep the image in your head: an ocean with no shores, roofed by ice, warmed from below.
An ocean with more water than ours, and no way for the sun to reach it.
Nothing about that lid is thin enough to see through.
If you poured Earth's oceans into it, you would still have room for another Earth's worth.
The moon is not a dead ball of ice, it is being worked on from the outside, every orbit.
That is the first surprise of this world: the heat comes from a neighbour, not from the star.
Enceladus is smaller, but the same three layers appear: ice, water, and rock.
Does a smaller world keep its ocean as easily? That is a question only the mission data can answer.
